steps.title: New objects, not mutations
steps.detail: React compares identities. Mutating in place updates the data and leaves the screen alone.
steps.example: current.map((t) => (t.id === id ? { ...t, completed: !t.completed } : t))

model_solution.key_principle: In React, immutability is not a style choice — it is the mechanism by which change is detected.
model_solution.great_looks_like: Add three tasks, tick one, delete another, hit refresh, and the screen is exactly as you left it.

questions.question: `useState(loadTasks)` vs `useState(loadTasks())` — what's the difference?
options: Passing the function defers the call to the first render only; calling it inline re-reads and re-parses localStorage on every single render, and only the first result is ever used
The function form is only valid inside useEffect
questions.explanation: Lazy initial state. React only uses the initial value once, but the expression you pass is evaluated every render — an easy, invisible performance leak.

questions.question: Why does the effect that writes to localStorage list `[tasks]` as its dependency?
options: So it runs after every render, which is what persistence needs
So it runs only when tasks actually changed — an empty array would write once and never again; omitting the array writes on every render
Dependency arrays are required by React and the contents are ignored
So it runs before the component mounts
questions.explanation: No array → every render. Empty array → mount only, so nothing after the first change is ever saved. [tasks] → exactly when the data changed.

questions.question: Why does toggling build a new object with `{ ...task, completed: !task.completed }` instead of assigning `task.completed = true`?
options: Direct assignment is a syntax error in strict mode
React compares by identity — mutating in place leaves the same object and array references, so React sees nothing changed and skips the re-render
It prevents the object being garbage collected
questions.explanation: Immutability is not stylistic here; it is the mechanism by which React detects change. Mutation produces the maddening 'the data updated but the screen didn't' bug.

questions.question: localStorage.getItem returns a string that isn't valid JSON. The solution wraps JSON.parse in try/catch. Why does that matter?
options: JSON.parse is asynchronous and can reject
A throw during initial state means the component never mounts — the whole app is bricked by one corrupt key until the user clears storage they don't know exists
localStorage requires exception handling by specification
questions.explanation: Storage is shared, persistent, and editable by anything on the origin — including an older version of your own app. Treat it as untrusted input.

questions.question: Which best describes the limits of localStorage for real applications?
options: It is encrypted and safe for auth tokens and personal data
It is synchronous (so it blocks the main thread), per-origin, capped at roughly 5MB, string-only, and readable by any script on the page — fine for preferences and drafts, wrong for secrets
It is shared across every site the user visits
questions.explanation: The 'readable by any script' part is the one that matters: any XSS or third-party tag can read it. Great for UI state, not a place for tokens.

explainer.situation: The capstone. Everything so far has been a piece of something; this is a small complete feature that a person could genuinely use. The new idea is persistence — state that outlives the page — and it brings with it two of React's most instructive traps: lazy initial state, and immutable updates.
explainer.outcome: A task list you can add to, tick off and delete from, which is exactly as you left it after a refresh.
explainer.preview:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ [ Write onboarding docs      ] [ Add ]   │
├──────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Ship the feature        [Done] [Delete]  │  ← task-item
│ ~~Fix the nav bug~~     [Done] [Delete]  │  ← completed: true
└──────────────────────────────────────────┘

localStorage['tasks'] =
  [{"id":1,"text":"Ship the feature","completed":false},
   {"id":2,"text":"Fix the nav bug","completed":true}]

  …and it is all still there after F5.

concepts.plain: A small key-value store the browser keeps per site, surviving reloads and restarts. Strings only — objects go in via JSON.stringify and come out via JSON.parse.
concepts.why: It is the simplest possible persistence, with real limits: synchronous (it blocks the main thread), around 5MB, and readable by any script on the page. Fine for preferences and drafts; never for tokens.

concepts.plain: Runs a function AFTER React has rendered. The dependency array controls when: `[tasks]` means 'after any render where tasks changed'.
concepts.why: Writing to localStorage during render would be a side effect in the middle of React's own work. Effects are where you reach outside React.

concepts.plain: `useState(loadTasks)` hands React the function to call once. `useState(loadTasks())` calls it yourself, on every single render, and React discards every result after the first.
concepts.why: React only uses the initial value once, but the expression you write is evaluated every render. With a localStorage read and a JSON.parse inside, that is real, invisible waste.

concepts.plain: Never change an object or array in place. Build a new one: spread into a new array to add, .map to a new object to change, .filter to a new array to remove.
concepts.why: React decides whether to re-render by comparing references. Mutating `task.completed` leaves the same object in the same array — React sees nothing changed and skips the render. The data updated and the screen did not.

concepts.plain: `setTasks(current => …)` hands you the latest state instead of whatever the closure captured.
concepts.why: It stays correct when several updates are batched together, or when the callback was created a render or two ago.

steps.title: Read localStorage once, safely
steps.plain: Write a function that reads and parses the stored tasks, returning an empty array if there is nothing or if it cannot be parsed. Pass that function to useState — do not call it.
steps.deeper: The try/catch is not defensive padding. Storage is shared across every script on the origin, persists indefinitely, and may hold something an older version of your own app wrote. A throw during initial state means the component never mounts — one corrupt key bricks the app until the user clears storage they do not know exists.

steps.title: Write back whenever the tasks change
steps.plain: One effect, depending on `tasks`. It runs after any render where the array changed, and saves it.
steps.deeper: The dependency array is the whole behaviour. No array → runs after every render, wasteful. `[]` → runs once on mount, so nothing you do afterwards is ever saved. `[tasks]` → exactly when the data changed. Getting this wrong produces persistence that appears to work until you reload.

steps.title: Add, ignoring empty input
steps.plain: Trim the text. If nothing is left, return without doing anything. Otherwise append a new task and clear the input.
steps.deeper: `Date.now()` alone is not a safe id — two tasks added in the same millisecond collide, and duplicate keys make React reuse the wrong node. In production, crypto.randomUUID(). Also note the spread builds a NEW array; `current.push(…)` would mutate and render nothing.

steps.title: Toggle by building a new object
steps.plain: `.map` over the tasks. For the one that matches, return a copy with completed flipped; return the others unchanged.
steps.deeper: This is the single most important line in the task. `task.completed = !task.completed` would update the data perfectly and change nothing on screen, because the array and every object in it still have the same identity. Returning the untouched tasks by reference is deliberate too — only what changed gets a new identity, so React re-renders only that row.

steps.title: Delete by filtering
steps.plain: `.filter` returns a new array without the matching task.
steps.deeper: Same principle as toggling: a new array, so React sees a change. It is also the clearest demonstration of why keys must be stable — with index keys, deleting the first row makes React believe every row below it changed.

mistakes: `useState(loadTasks())` instead of `useState(loadTasks)` — re-reads and re-parses storage on every render.
Mutating `task.completed` in place: the data changes and the screen does not.
`useEffect(…, [])` for the save, so only the initial empty array is ever written.
Storing the array without JSON.stringify — localStorage coerces it to the string "[object Object]".
Not trimming before the empty check, so a task made of spaces gets added.
`key={index}` on the list, which breaks visibly as soon as you delete from the middle.
further: Add filters — all / active / completed — and derive the visible list during render rather than storing it as a fourth piece of state.
Try useReducer instead of three separate setTasks calls. This is the size of feature where a reducer starts to pay for itself.
Listen for the `storage` event and watch two tabs stay in sync — it is about five lines and genuinely satisfying.
Read about optimistic updates: render the change immediately, then reconcile with the server, and roll back if it fails. It is what makes good apps feel instant.

assessment.title: Frontend Developer — Final Assessment
assessment.description: Fifty questions across everything the simulation covered: semantic HTML, CSS layout, the DOM and events, asynchronous JavaScript, React, accessibility, and the judgement calls behind the code you wrote. Difficulty ramps from fundamentals to senior-level trade-offs.

questions.question: Which element correctly wraps the primary content of a page, excluding site-wide headers and footers?
questions.explanation: <main> is the landmark for the page's primary content, and there should be exactly one per page.

questions.question: What is the difference between <section> and <div>?
options: <section> is a thematic grouping that normally has a heading; <div> carries no meaning and exists purely for styling or scripting hooks
<section> can only be used once per page
questions.explanation: If you cannot name the section with a heading, a <div> is usually the honest choice.

questions.question: Which attribute pairs a <label> with its input?
questions.explanation: <label for="email"> binds to <input id="email">. Clicking the label then focuses the field — and screen readers announce the label with it.

questions.question: A button that only shows an icon needs which of the following?
options: An accessible name, via visually-hidden text or aria-label — otherwise it is announced as just 'button'
A title attribute, which is sufficient on its own
questions.explanation: title is inconsistently announced and invisible to touch users. Visually-hidden text or aria-label is the reliable fix.

questions.question: What does the `alt` attribute do when an image fails to load?
options: Nothing, it is only for screen readers
The browser displays the alt text in place of the image, so the meaning survives a broken URL
questions.explanation: It serves both assistive technology and every user on a flaky connection.

questions.question: Which is the correct heading structure for a page?
options: h1, then h3, then h2, ordered by visual size
One h1, with h2s beneath it and h3s beneath those — the levels describe nesting, not size
Headings in any order, since CSS controls appearance
questions.explanation: Heading level is document structure. Style it however you like; do not skip levels to get a font size.

questions.question: What is the accessibility tree?
options: A visualisation of your component hierarchy in DevTools
A parallel structure the browser derives from the DOM, exposing roles, names and states to assistive technology
The list of focusable elements only
questions.explanation: It is what a screen reader actually reads. Semantic HTML populates it correctly for free; divs populate it with nothing.

questions.question: Which layout method is designed for one-dimensional distribution along a single axis?
questions.explanation: Flexbox: one axis. Grid: two. Reaching for the right one first saves a lot of fighting.

questions.question: `justify-content` in a default flex row controls what?
questions.explanation: In a row, justify-content is the main (horizontal) axis and align-items is the cross (vertical) axis. They swap with flex-direction: column.

questions.question: `box-sizing: border-box` changes what?
options: Adds a border to every element
Makes width include padding and border, so a 200px box stays 200px once you add padding
Removes the default margin on body
questions.explanation: The default content-box makes padding push the total size outwards — the reason `* { box-sizing: border-box }` opens most stylesheets.

questions.question: Which selector has the highest specificity?
questions.explanation: An id contributes far more specificity than any number of classes or elements. It is also why over-using ids makes stylesheets hard to override.

questions.question: What does `1fr` mean in a grid track definition?
options: One fraction of the leftover free space in the container
questions.explanation: fr distributes what's left after fixed sizes and gaps are accounted for.

questions.question: Why prefer `rem` over `px` for font sizes?
options: rem scales with the user's root font size, so someone who has enlarged their browser text gets larger text; px ignores that preference
questions.explanation: It is an accessibility default, not a stylistic one.

questions.question: A `position: absolute` element positions itself relative to what?
options: Its nearest ancestor with a position other than static — or the initial containing block if there is none
questions.explanation: Forgetting `position: relative` on the intended parent is why absolutely positioned elements so often fly to the corner of the page.

questions.question: What does `gap` do that margins on children do not?
options: It spaces items only between each other, with no leading or trailing space to strip off, and it never collapses
It adds padding inside each item
questions.explanation: No more :last-child { margin-right: 0 }.

questions.question: Which media feature respects a user who has asked their OS to reduce animation?
questions.explanation: Honouring it is not optional for users with vestibular disorders — motion can cause real nausea.

questions.question: What does `querySelectorAll` return?
options: A static NodeList — array-like, with forEach, but without map or filter until you spread it
questions.explanation: `Array.from(nodes)` or `[...nodes]` when you need real array methods.

questions.question: What is the difference between `==` and `===`?
options: == coerces types before comparing ('1' == 1 is true); === requires the types to match
questions.explanation: Default to ===. The coercion table for == has genuine surprises in it.

questions.question: Which values are falsy in JavaScript?
options: Empty arrays and empty objects as well
questions.explanation: Note what is NOT there: [] and {} are both truthy, which surprises people checking for 'empty'.

questions.question: `const team = []; team.push('Ada');` — why is this allowed?
options: It is a bug in the specification
const binds the variable to a value; it does not freeze the object. The binding cannot be reassigned, but the array's contents can change
questions.explanation: Use Object.freeze if you actually need immutability.

questions.question: What is a closure?
options: A function that has been garbage collected
A function that keeps access to the variables of the scope it was created in, even after that scope has finished executing
A way of closing a browser tab from script
questions.explanation: It is why an event listener can still read a variable defined around it — and why stale values in React callbacks happen.

questions.question: `setTimeout(fn, 0)` runs `fn` when?
options: After the current synchronous work finishes and the call stack clears — 0 is a minimum delay, not a promise of immediacy
questions.explanation: The event loop in one question: the timer is queued, not run.

questions.question: What is the difference between `null` and `undefined`?
options: undefined means a value was never assigned; null is an explicit, deliberate 'no value'
null is a syntax error in strict mode
undefined can only appear in function parameters
questions.explanation: typeof null === 'object' is a famous, unfixable historical bug in the language.

questions.question: What does `async` in front of a function do?
options: Runs the function on a background thread
Makes it return a promise and permits `await` inside it — the work still runs on the single main thread
questions.explanation: JavaScript remains single-threaded. async is about scheduling, not parallelism.

questions.question: Two independent API calls, and you need both before rendering. What is the efficient approach?
options: Start both, then `await Promise.all([a, b])` so they overlap
Call them inside a for loop
questions.explanation: Sequential awaits on independent work turns 200ms + 200ms into 400ms for no reason.

questions.question: What does the optional chaining operator `?.` do?
options: Short-circuits to undefined if the value before it is null or undefined, instead of throwing
Marks a property as nullable in TypeScript only
questions.explanation: `user?.profile?.name` — pair it with `??` when you also want a fallback.

questions.question: Event delegation means:
options: Passing events between components as props
Attaching one listener to a common ancestor and using event.target to work out which descendant was hit — so dynamically added children work without new listeners
Delegating events to a web worker
questions.explanation: One listener on a list beats one per row, and it keeps working when rows are added later.

questions.question: What does `useState` return?
options: A pair: the current value and a setter function
A promise resolving to the value
questions.explanation: `const [value, setValue] = useState(initial)` — array destructuring, which is why you can name them anything.

questions.question: Calling a state setter does what?
options: Updates the variable immediately, in place
Schedules a re-render; the variable in the current scope keeps its old value until the next render
questions.explanation: Reading state right after setting it and seeing the old value is not a bug — it's the render model.

questions.question: When does `useEffect(fn, [])` run?
questions.explanation: Empty deps → mount only. The returned cleanup then runs on unmount.

questions.question: What does the function returned from useEffect do?
options: It is the cleanup — React runs it before the next effect and on unmount, which is where you remove listeners, clear timers and abort requests
It provides the effect's return value to the component
questions.explanation: Missing cleanup is how you get listeners stacking up and setState-after-unmount warnings.

questions.question: Why must hooks not be called inside conditions or loops?
options: React matches hooks to their state by call order; a hook that is sometimes skipped shifts every subsequent hook onto the wrong state
Conditions are not allowed in function components at all
questions.explanation: The order is the identity. This is exactly what the rules-of-hooks lint rule protects.

questions.question: What is 'lifting state up'?
options: Moving state to the closest common ancestor when two components need to share it, and passing it down as props
Moving state from a child to the browser URL
questions.explanation: It is the standard first answer to 'these two components need the same data', before reaching for any library.

questions.question: Which is a valid reason to use `useRef`?
options: Storing state that should trigger a re-render
Holding a mutable value that must survive renders WITHOUT causing one — a DOM node, a timer id, a previous value
questions.explanation: Changing .current never re-renders. That is the point, and also the trap if you expected UI to update.

questions.question: A controlled component is one where:
options: React state is the single source of truth for the input's value
It uses a ref to read the value on submit
questions.explanation: The uncontrolled alternative — reading a ref on submit — is legitimate, just a different trade-off.

questions.question: Why does React need `key` on list items?
options: To match elements to their previous instances across renders, so it can move rather than rebuild them and keep internal state on the right row
It is only required in development
questions.explanation: Reconciliation. Index keys break as soon as the list can be reordered or filtered.

questions.question: `{count && <Badge />}` renders '0' when count is 0. What is the fix?
options: Both the explicit boolean and the ternary work
questions.explanation: React skips false/null/undefined but renders the number 0. Either fix is fine; the explicit comparison reads better.

questions.question: What problem does `React.memo` address?
options: A component re-rendering when its props have not actually changed — it skips the render if a shallow prop comparison finds them equal
questions.explanation: Measure first. Wrapping everything in memo has its own cost and often hides the real problem — an unstable prop identity.

questions.question: Why can passing an inline arrow function as a prop defeat React.memo?
options: A new function object is created on every render, so the shallow prop comparison always sees a change
memo does not compare function props
Arrow functions cannot be passed as props
questions.explanation: This is the problem useCallback exists to solve — and the reason memo without stable props achieves nothing.

questions.question: Fetching in useEffect, the component unmounts before the response arrives. What is the correct handling?
options: Abort the request or set a cancelled flag in the cleanup, so you do not update state on an unmounted component
Move the fetch into the render body
questions.explanation: AbortController in the cleanup is the modern answer, and it also stops a stale response overwriting a fresh one.

questions.question: A <div> with an onClick handler is not usable by keyboard. What does making it a real <button> give you?
options: Focusability, Enter/Space activation, the correct announced role, and disabled semantics — all of which you would otherwise have to rebuild by hand
Nothing, they are equivalent with role="button"
questions.explanation: role="button" plus tabindex plus key handlers gets you most of the way — using the element gets you all of it for free.

questions.question: What does `aria-live="polite"` do?
options: Queues the announcement for when the screen reader next pauses — right for status updates, whereas role="alert" interrupts
questions.explanation: Polite for 'saved', 'filtered to 12 results'. Assertive/alert for errors that block progress.

questions.question: Minimum contrast ratio for normal-size body text under WCAG AA?
questions.explanation: 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text. AAA raises it to 7:1.

questions.question: Why should focus be visible?
options: Keyboard users navigate by focus — removing the outline without replacing it makes the interface impossible to use without a mouse
It is only needed for form fields
questions.explanation: `outline: none` with no replacement is one of the most damaging one-liners in CSS. Use :focus-visible for a considered style.

questions.question: Which most directly improves Largest Contentful Paint?
options: Optimising and correctly sizing the largest above-the-fold image, and not blocking its discovery behind JavaScript
Moving all CSS into inline style attributes
questions.explanation: LCP is usually a hero image or a heading. Find what the element actually is before optimising anything.

questions.question: What does `loading="lazy"` on an do?
options: Tells the browser it may defer loading until the image is near the viewport, saving bandwidth on long pages
Delays the load by a fixed 500ms
questions.explanation: Do not use it on your LCP image — deferring the thing the user came to see makes the metric worse.

questions.question: Debouncing a search input means:
options: Waiting until typing pauses for a set interval before firing, so ten keystrokes cause one request rather than ten
Cancelling the request if it takes too long
questions.explanation: Throttling is the neighbouring idea: at most one call per interval, for things like scroll handlers.

questions.question: Why is user-supplied content unsafe to write with innerHTML?
options: It parses as markup, so embedded HTML and event-handler attributes execute — the core mechanism of cross-site scripting
questions.explanation: React escapes by default, which is why dangerouslySetInnerHTML is named the way it is.

questions.question: A colleague's PR adds a 400KB date library to format one timestamp. What is the most useful review comment?
options: Approve — readability matters more than bundle size
Ask whether Intl.DateTimeFormat, already in every browser, covers the case — and if not, whether a modular import would pull in only what is used
Ask them to lazy-load the whole library
questions.explanation: Lead with the question, not the verdict. The platform often already has it, and the answer is a two-line diff.

questions.question: You inherit a page where every interactive element is a styled <div>. What is the highest-value first fix?
options: Convert them to real <button> and <a> elements — that single change restores keyboard access, focus order and correct announcements across the whole page
questions.explanation: All four are worth doing. Element semantics is the one that fixes the largest number of failures per line changed.

simulation.title: Enterprise SaaS Sales Representative
simulation.description: A full sales cycle at Nimbus CRM: qualify a lead, research the account, send cold outreach, run a discovery call, work the deal in a real CRM, handle objections, write a proposal, and close.

company.name: Nimbus CRM
company.about: Nimbus CRM builds an AI-powered sales platform for mid-market and enterprise sales teams. The sales org is expanding into industrial and manufacturing accounts, which is exactly the kind of deal you're about to run.

onboarding.intro:
Welcome to the team — glad to have you on board.

Here's how I work: I hand my reps a real deal, start to finish, and I expect you to run the whole cycle yourself — qualify it, research it, work it, and close it. I'm not going to hover over every email, but I will read your CRM, your transcripts, and your proposal the way I'd read any rep's on my team.

Your first deal is Atlas Forge Manufacturing — a real inbound lead that just came in. Let's get you into it.
learn: Qualifying an inbound lead and defending your scoring with real reasoning
Researching an account like a rep who actually wants to win the deal
Writing cold outreach that earns a reply, not a delete
Running a discovery call that uncovers real pain, budget, and timeline
Working a deal in a real CRM — accounts, contacts, opportunities, pipeline
Handling real objections with substance, not scripted reassurance
Building a proposal that makes an honest business case
Closing — demo, signature, negotiation, and a clean handoff to onboarding

offer.title: Enterprise SaaS Sales Representative — Job Simulation
offer.body: We're delighted to offer you a place on the Nimbus CRM Enterprise SaaS Sales Representative Job Simulation. You'll run one real deal start to finish — lead qualification, research, outreach, a discovery call, working the pipeline in a real CRM, objection handling, a proposal, and the close — building the exact skills an enterprise sales rep needs on the job. By accepting, you're committing to give each stage a genuine attempt and to learn by doing. We're excited to see you close.

steps.title: Weigh firmographics against buying intent
steps.detail: $85M revenue and 420 employees clears any minimum-deal-size bar comfortably — but the stronger signal is the inbound demo request plus a new VP publicly asking for better pipeline visibility. Score the intent higher than firmographics alone would suggest.

steps.title: Read the pain points as the deal's actual shape
steps.detail: Chronic pipeline blindness and a blown forecast aren't abstract — they're the exact wedge Nimbus solves. Note that explicitly instead of just restating the fields.

steps.title: Write reasoning a manager could act on without re-reading the file
steps.detail: State the score, the one or two facts driving it, and the recommended priority — in that order.

model_solution.key_principle: A lead score without written reasoning isn't a decision — it's a guess with a number on it.
model_solution.great_looks_like: leadScore ~75-85, buyingIntent High, priority High — reasoning that names the one or two facts actually driving the score.

Company profile: Atlas Forge Manufacturing, ~420 employees, ~$85M revenue, founded 1984 in Youngstown OH. Core business is CNC-machined components for automotive OEMs, now expanding into EV battery-enclosure parts.

Pain points: No shared pipeline visibility; deals tracked in personal spreadsheets; Q3 forecast missed by 34%; the new EV line means reps are prospecting a buyer persona with no existing playbook.

Risks: HubSpot was already evaluated and rejected as too marketing-focused — don't repeat that positioning mistake. A local ERP vendor is pitching a bundled CRM module as a competing, and possibly cheaper-feeling, bid.

tasks.title: Stage 3 — Cold Outreach
tasks.objective: Write a cold email that earns a reply.
tasks.briefing: Turn your research into a cold email — a clear subject line, a personalized body that shows you did your homework, and one specific call to action.
hints: Lead with their problem, not your product.
One CTA. Not "let me know if you have any questions."
Reference something specific from your research — generic emails get deleted.

steps.title: Open with their problem, not your product
steps.detail: Reference the pipeline-visibility pain point from research in the first sentence, before Nimbus is even mentioned.

steps.title: Personalize with one specific, real detail
steps.detail: The new VP of Sales hire or the EV product line launch — either proves you did the research, a generic template can't fake it.

steps.title: End with exactly one low-friction CTA
steps.detail: "Worth 15 minutes Thursday?" beats "let me know if you have any questions."

model_solution.great_looks_like: A prospect reading it thinks "this person actually looked at my company" within the first two sentences.
model_solution.example_solution:
Subject: Pipeline visibility for Atlas Forge's new EV line?

Hi Marcus — noticed Atlas Forge brought on a new VP of Sales recently, and that you're expanding into EV battery-enclosure components. Teams making that kind of move often hit a wall with spreadsheet-tracked pipelines — forecast accuracy tends to fall apart right when the business is changing fastest.

Nimbus CRM helps industrial sales teams get real pipeline visibility without forcing reps into a heavier system than they'll actually use. Worth 15 minutes this week to see if it's relevant to what you're building?

CTA: Worth 15 minutes this week?

tasks.briefing: You're live with the prospect now. Build rapport, ask real discovery questions, and come out of this call understanding their challenges, goals, budget, and timeline — not just pitching features.
hints: Open with a question, not a pitch.
Ask about the cost of the status quo, not just their goals.
If they mention a specific number or date, that's a buying signal — don't let it pass by.

steps.title: Open with a question, not a pitch
steps.detail: "Walk me through how deals get tracked today?" beats any Nimbus talking point in the first minute.

model_solution.key_principle: Discovery calls exist to earn information, not to deliver a pitch — the rep who talks least often learns most.
model_solution.great_looks_like: Your call notes contain a specific budget range or figure, a timeline, and at least one pain point in Marcus's own words, not your paraphrase of it.
model_solution.example_solution: Example opening: "Before I say anything about what we do — walk me through how a deal moves from first contact to closed today?" Then follow up on whatever gap he names (usually visibility or forecast accuracy) with "what does that actually cost you when it happens?" rather than jumping to a feature pitch.

tasks.title: Stage 7 — Proposal
tasks.objective: Put together a proposal that makes the business case.
tasks.briefing: Write the proposal you'd actually send: the business problem, your recommended solution, an implementation plan, the expected ROI, a timeline, and pricing.
hints: Tie the ROI number back to something the buyer told you in discovery.
Implementation plan should reduce risk, not just list steps.
Pricing should match what you scoped in the opportunity — don't contradict your own CRM.

steps.title: Tie the ROI section to something Marcus or Elena actually said
steps.detail: The 34% forecast miss is a real, quantifiable number to build the ROI case around — don't invent a generic industry statistic.

steps.title: Make the implementation plan reduce risk, not just list steps
steps.detail: A phased rollout (pilot with one team, then expand) reads as lower-risk than a big-bang company-wide switch.

steps.title: Match the pricing to what's in the CRM opportunity
steps.detail: If the proposal number doesn't match your own CRM record, it undermines the whole document's credibility.
